title: Just because I'm painfully obsessed with Chazelle's BABYLON...

commenti.body: [removed]

Babylon is a schizophrenic piece of crap. I want my $17 back for the ticket, and the $20 in gas to drive into the city to watch it. Anyone who knows what happened when the silents went to talkies knows the plot instantly. Who made it after the silents? Gloria Swanson and Joan Crawford. Like, we know odds are low for most and they’re going to be winnowed out. Babylon is a cheap exercise in excess. And the director was projecting with the “your time is up,” monologue. Babylon is meandering when it’s not predictable. There’s no need for Tobey McGuire to be there, no need for the underground fight club crap. Babylon has beautiful moments and insufferable moments. It’s both beautiful and a turd.

It's a fascinating movie to me because I feel it could have been much better. Firstly the dialogue doesn't sound 20s. Robbie swears like she's in a Sam Jackson gangster flick!

I'd have cut out the elephant poop etc, and focused on the love story between Nelly and Manny. My rewrite idea changes Pitt's character. Currently him and Robbie are male and female versions of the same character: silent movie stars who struggle with talkies. Her arc is more developed as she goes from unknown to star to tragedy.

What if instead, he plays Chairman William Hays and it focuses on the introduction of the Hays Code? It contrasts the wild, decadent pre-Code era which was accepting with the strict moralistic era that followed - set against the backdrop of the Depression.

Some of the good bits of the film could be retained: maybe the black trumpeters are a mixed-race band Hays orders Manny to split up (the Hays Code demanded racial segregation). Lady Fu is fired. Then Hays demands he removes Nelly as a symbol of the old debauched Hollywood and Manny has to choose between his Producer career and his love for her.

As it was the film tries to do too much, it would have done better as a more tightly focused story. But there's potential in a love story between an out-of-control star and a Producer who has to choose between her and his career.

My take: the first half was ridiculously excessive, the second half was excessively ridiculous. I was loving everything about the filmmaking but as of one point (maybe when she fights a snake at a party?) I began to care less and less, and the part with Tobey Maguire was the lowest point of my investment in the movie. 

I get why it worked for some people, but as a whole it reeeeally didn't work for me. Plus, I HATE that whenever I think of that movie one of the few shots that will come to my mind is the one from Avatar from the ending montage.
The Tobey Maguire subplot is such a ripoff of Boogie Nights it’s not even funny.

Chazelle definitely bit more than he could chew with this one.

First of all, too many characters with unclear way of why the audience should care about them. I think going from movies with clear leads to this one so abruptly didn't make him understand how to develop that kind of human depth necessary: we see all these great actors framed in the most notable way, as if the fact that the shots are beautiful and that it's about "MOVIES!" was enough for us to keep watching in AVE. It works for the first part scene, but it gets as boring as it could with every meaningless subplot. I say meaningless because, again, there is little reason and meaning for these episodes to exist and be shown, and there are so many! The Asian actress, the black trumpet guy, Tobey Maguire ffs...

Secondly, the message is quite off. It wants us to feel the love of cinema in spite of being made by awful people. Ok, I get it, but perhaps you definitely need to focus more on this aspect and make us feel what the protagonist is feeling. Who is the protagonist, again? Pitt and Robbie are almost one same character of which we never get to see the real intentions or desires. Pitt definitely does more through sheer aura and charisma while Robbie being much younger and less experienced simply doesn't have. Manny instead is a protagonist sacrificed to this movie: his desire and what should be the fire working in favour of cinema is all relegated to a coked out monologue at the beginning of the film. From there on, it's just shit apparently? So no idea why at the end we should feel what he's feeling. 

Talking about the end, it does feel too montage-y. Like, it's clear it was not the real ending, because that alone was absolutely insipid. Because of the aforementioned reasons, you get to the ending moments that you don't connect at all with Manny's emotions. The episodes have been at this point Too many, too dark and too disconnected with the audience emotionally for us to give a damn, and he resorted to something very very film school which is to just throw a parade of frames to the audience in order to impress. It felt desperate. 

Lastly, the script and the acting was so unfocused. For every camera movement that felt as if it was over qualified for the assignment, there was a dissonance between the characters, the context, the immersion... Robbie's character becomes way too unrealistic and she goes full DiCaprio on this one, and we are led to believe that the only reason Manny falls in love with her is because of the sex she exudes through dancing and swearing. If she was supposed to be, in Manny's eyes, a parallel to cinema, then his love for her, their connection, and thus the validity of these characters to the audience, are all as shallow as they get. Manny's actor tried but again, the script gives us Very little reason to root for him. Pitt felt the only one fully understanding how to do little things for his character in order for us to care, but the script gives him little to do after the first act. 

So many things going off for a movie that felt way too thought out in not so relevant parts and little left to the human side of it, the spectator. The cinematography is beautiful, but it's too showy in relation of the characters, definitely felt as if he was trying every single trick of film schools and it's weird since even whiplash and especially first man are much more restrained in that matter. It needed a rewrite or, given this edit, at least twenty to forty minutes less. The length feels purely as a way to give itself self importance and is the biggest flag for the self indulgence that ruined the film.

Epic soundtrack tho.

> elephant poop 

To me, the fact it started on this was meant to say 'yeah, it's going to be gross at times'. Like a warning. If you couldn't take it, then leave.

A bit like how he stated he cold started La La Land with a singing number, then there was none for at least half an hour, so it didn't get too jarring when it got to a singing part.

I’m so happy when I see someone take the words out of my mouth. I am so bad at finding the right words to say, and this is it. I love this film so much and not everyone does. I agree that the first impression is strange. Even I was initially turned off by it. But that party sequence drew me in. Perfectly paced, a great introduction to our characters, and setting the tone—this is going to be dirty, absurd, and chaotic. The ending felt a bit pretentious but I loved it. I loved this movie so much.

I think the whole movie is. It's not that deep. It's boogie Nights with worse pacing and far less character work so you don't care about anyone on the screen. Boogie Nights showed Dirks decline into drugs. Babylon just randomly says "oh yeah, Robbie has a huge gambling problem and it's ruining her career I guess?". 

The director wanted to spend too much time on those two or three opening scenes that he seemed to have cut out any of the character building that's essential to movies like this.

I don’t know how anyone can take seriously a film that takes its only black character of note (Sidney Palmer), thinly sketches him until a trite “racism is bad” kicker and then completely drops him from the rest of the film as if his only point in existing was as a vehicle for a sentiment that 5 year olds would find obvious (or maybe as a means for the director to showcase his progressive bona fides). It is a very badly written movie, particularly in terms of characterization. And it completely rips off Boogie Nights.

I just think the movie would have been better without the poop, the inhuman amounts of puke, the rat eating etc. I get the negative reaction a lot of people had to it. A much better movie was trying to get out of this - cut out the yucky bits and focus on the Manny/Nelly relationship as the 20s become the 30s.

I like some parts of Babylon but it’s baffling to me that the guy that made two! movies about artists sacrificing their personal lives to excel in their career somehow messed up the third time around. It was kind of a weird choice they made to have Brad Pitt’s character almost never interact with Margot Robbie’s character; I get that the lead was Manuel (I forget the actor) but I feel like he was too much of a blank slate for me to care about him. Margot was fine but she also seemed too static throughout the film for me to care about her. 

I agree that it seemed like he wrote the opening of the film and then had no idea what to do for the next 3 hours. I feel like Chazelle got scared from the “white savior” backlash from La La Land but then forgot to give any of the side characters something to actually do. I feel like they could’ve merged Manny and the Sidney the trumpeter’s character and Margot and the cabaret dancer’s character (and maybe integrated Brad Pitt into the narrative more because his only real purpose to any of the other characters iirc is to give Manny a job) because splitting the narrative across 5 leads who are all super underwritten made the movie way more bloated than it should’ve been
I'd say he treats all the characters that way, not just the black character.

The problem in this approach is that it doesn't give you a good reason to fall in love with something that gets ugly. Hence why the ending and the general contrast between loving films made by shitty people just doesn't work.

>Pitt and Robbie are almost one same character of which we never get to see the real intentions or desires.

When I emphasized on the "it's bigger than you" phrase, I meant that all this characters are seeking to be part of something that is "bigger than them".

I believe Robert Daniels relatively sums it up in his [letterboxd review](https://boxd.it/3zrBxz), calling Babylon a *"fascinating critique on the ways the white capitalistic greed of Hollywood forced (and still forces) assimilation onto the dreams of the marginalized and then forces them to turn into each other."*

These characters become something less of who they are, and they surrender their own selves for something that's as promising and as murderus: their image being captured on film, a "fossil of an emotion experienced in real life, now belonging to the Hollywood apparatus."

Nellie LeRoy (Margot Robbie) needs to feel validated, she calls for attention, yet she simply can't negate her own life backgrounds when facing Hollywood constrains.

Manny feels worthless without this big-thing: Hollywood, the image, etc. At the end of the film, when he's about to be killed, he seeks for mercy dispariging his own self as "just a mexican", because moments before he was trying to fit Hollywood's hegemony lying about his background when saying he was from Spain.

Their relationship is difficult to define.

Jack Conrad (Brad Pitt) achieved to be part of this big-thing, as what cost? Fakeness. He doesn't know love in his life. Right from his introduction at the party, we know what his issue is: lack of sincerity from the people around him; strangers in the middle of a party reaching for him, providing quick validation but ultimate emptiness. His acting is a "simulacrum of a real emotion", and that's all he has. Once he looses it, it's over for him.

The fact that the asian and black characters fall under this reductive characterizations, are very telling of their place in Hollywood's picture. We see Sidney (Jovan Adepo), though, as someone who stands strong for his own values and self-worth. There's no "thing bigger than him", his real emotions and life experiences are reduced to fit Hollywood's image.

In my opinion, Babylon's story is tightly crafted, which as you say, may lack of emotion. There a distance between the audience and the characters. Maybe Chazelle made a wise decision showing us glimpses of who they are—we'll never fully understand this personalities, just the compressed emotions found in a Hollywood picture; makes me think of Nellie's single-tear captured on celluloid, which is a close-up unaware of the disasters going on in that set, and unaware of Nellie's background for that tear: her crying was a cause of her thinking of her home, but we never get much more insight of it because in the big-picture... it simply doesn't matter. She's just there to be swallowed and spitten.

In a deeper reading, Babylon doesn't spend too much time on its characters because, as I just wrote in another comment, they do not matter in the bigger picture. Chazelle keeps it cold: when Nellie's asked how she's able to cry so much, she says "I just think of home", and we quickly cut to nonsensensical excess. These characters do not matter in Hollywood's bigger picture: they are there to be swallowed and spitten, and any real emotion they may show is quickly fed up to the Hollywood apparatus, just like an out-of-context single-tear.
Thats just a typical hw night back then
I mean, read it however you want, it doesn't make for a great movie when you don't care about what's happening to any one.

> I want my $17 back for the ticket, and the $20 in gas to drive into the city to watch it. Anyone who knows what happened when the silents went to talkies knows the plot instantly.

So why'd you go?

>it doesn't make for a great movie when you don't care about what's happening to any one.

It's much more subjective stuff, for sure. Some people were totally enthralled, some others didn't care at all (and it's alright, Babylon is a self-aware film—it wants to call as much attention as possible while dealing with a niche subject—once it does get the attentiom, it punishes itself, throws itself out of a bridge).

But Chazelle's films are, in their core, nothing but the fading.

Babylon's sad trumpets can be heard from miles away.

Bravo, that's a great write-up. I like to describe the movie as a movie the youngest Oscar winner for directing would make. But he made First Man after that, so what gives? He is extremely talented, it's obvious, even here, but he reverted from mature to more edgy filmmaking. The script is weak and all over the place. His knowledge of Hollywood history is not sufficient. The final montage from Lumières to Avatar is one of the worst things I saw this year.

Babylon is a really really cool movie, which takes it to good, bordering on great, but I think the movie self-engrandizes itself a bit too much. The movie doesn't pull the reigns back enough at a few moments.

The elephant shitting scene is a perfect example. It's a funny scene and making it the first scene of the movie makes a statement: 'this movie is going to be over-the-top' or 'this is not going to be an easy movie'. But the scene just goes on too long. We get it, haha funny, we don't need a 5 minute scene of an elephant shitting. There's a couple more sequences like that, at least one more I can think of, that is just a little gluttonous/overzealous.

Babylon
Lots of characters get dropped suddenly, like the female director. There's a message there about fame is fickle, but for a film we really want full characterization.

My Letterboxd review/analysis of the film: https://boxd.it/4R3fsT

By hour three, it becomes clear that Damien Chazelle set out to make the last movie ever made. 

One last film to close the great conversation started over 100 years ago, to represent the roses and thorns of a medium, an industry, and a lifetime for many. To do that means you’re going to need to pack a lot in, even with over three hours to work with, so to paraphrase myself upon seeing *Avatar: The Way of Water*, few movies have movie’d as hard as Babylon - an electric whirlwind that transposes Sodom and Gomorrah atop the early days of Hollywood as its first generations of stars rise and fall.

>There's a message there about fame is fickle

Yes, and not only "fame" exactly, but your whole role as an artist in an industry that's just there to swallow you and spit you at anytime. Characters are left ignored, and the film is rather cold towards them because in the big picture they don't matter. As I've commented earlier, we get glimpses of our characters, like Nellie saying she's able to cry fast by "thinking of home", and quickly cutting to nonsensical excess in which are characters and the audience sink in. True emotion coming from them is reduced, simplified into 8mm prints, like Nellie's single-tear, or Manny and Nellie's kiss at the end.

"The fact that the asian and black characters fall under this reductive characterizations, are very telling of their place in Hollywood's picture. We see Sidney (Jovan Adepo), though, as someone who stands strong for his own values and self-worth. There's no "thing bigger than him", his real emotions and life experiences are reduced to fit Hollywood's image."

So, you are adding a lot of points that sprawl from one aspect to the movie to the other and it's difficult to answer you, but first I wanted to start from here. I really don't think that having such one dimensional characters is in the interest of any director, with clear cut exceptions (Paul Verhoeven and satire?). It's pretty clear that,if you want to read more than "undeveloped character that was further cut down from the final edit", some people may say you're reaching. Of course they are a way to present the racial aspect of Hollywood in those years, but in this movie it just feels too much and too little at the same time. Those two characters could be a film on their own. Hell, Manny's Mexican origins could have been enough on that part.

You make a good and huge argument with the "larger than them" but I feel like you're kind of using it as a get out of jail free card. That kind of feeling simply does not stop the writer, in this case the writer director, to develop the character and make the audience care for it, no matter how much you see into it. I don't think in chazelle's previous movies we are given their whole backstory going along their personal diary, it's just a matter on focus and how you do it, and here it was too sprawling, too messy. 

I don't want to suggest the movie is total garbage, on the contrary, it's a bit of a rushed and wasted opportunity. The "characters crushed by something bigger than them" is s very valid and interesting perspective, I just think it wasn't developed enough and properly, just like the characters themselves, and if that happens in a three hour movie where you do have to feel a little something about them, you can only drag yourself to an emotionally detached ending. I feel like Robbie and Pott's character where more than enough for a film, but he kinda needed Manny to insert his own perspective and something to tie the two, but, together with all the threads and shock value, made the movie loose his focus. And that's why they had to rush a lazy montage ending.

I get what it was trying to do. It's ambitious, and a memorable film. I'm glad it was made. But I understand why it didn't do well at the box office - its message isn't  what would interest most people to actually pay to see it.

In general, the editing here is a big problem. Not the editor's fault, in fact, I pity him as if he was held hostage. I can't believe he wouldn't have cut some parts if he were given the freedom to. If I recall correctly, the ending montage was an idea of his, which I can believe, but it just feels so desperate and distracting to put such recent movies. Couldn't they have done something only with movies released up to that year in history? Or it wasn't colorful enough? You see, they had to have color, so they could mesh red green and blue, you see, they are the RGB, I've just learnt that in school....

That's deliberate.  Hollywood got less diverse with the advent of sound.  Women directors and minorities were pushed out for whiter/ more male casts and crews.  There's a great interview with Chazelle and Olivia Hamilton, his wife who produced Babylon and played the women director Ruth, where they talk about making all the background characters at the various parties deliberately less diverse as it went on.  The film takes a deliberately archetypal approach with it's characters, but I'd argue it still layers a fair bit of complexity into all of them.  All four of it's main aspirants have fairly well defined wants and needs that tie well into their various endings.
I didn’t know it was going to suck.

>It's pretty clear that,if you want to read more than "undeveloped character that was further cut down from the final edit", some people may say you're reaching.

Nah I get it. It's pretty easy to say that Chazelle simply pigeonholed side characters into basic characterization. I really need to rewatch the film again to have clearer conclusions.

I always try to read films outside of our usual ideas about how a film should be, how it should be told (and that's why I try to do when I post about Babylon on r/truefilm—I want to encourage over-the-top discussions).

And for example, when I first watched Chantal Akerman's *News from Home*, or Cassavetes *Faces*, I said "WOW". I realized that movies are allowed to be exhausting, to cause real irritation, to bother the spectator. They are experiments; Akerman and Cassavetes understand that any emotion or sensation from the spectator is allowed when watching a film, and it's okay, and I believe Chazelle takes from that for BABYLON when I call it a "rorschach test".

So I try to question those feelings of detachedness, of confusion—if the movie feels rushed, if the movie steels from older works in cinema, etc. What does Damien, an expert crowd-pleaser filmmaker, try to do when opening a movie with an elephant shitting on screen. Why would he risk so absurdly his career with this joke?

Maybe it's a too wild outside-the-box criticism, especially since you don't know if the filmmaker's intentions were there or not (doesn't really matter though).

So about detachment... Idk. On one hand, it seems he wants to get you emotional by the ending. On the other, he wants to cut between emotions by brutally cutting from a suicide to Manny and Nellie's storyline in an already exhausting point of the story (following the Cassavetes and Akerman style on seeked exhaustion—Chazelle wants to sink the audience into the excess and the ultime feelings of dejection).

And the other hand, I write too much, sorry lol. I'll watch it again and come back to r/truefilm with clearer thoughts.

First of all, don't worry about writing too much, but rather on writing in a way that one can respond to you, dividing arguments. 

I really don't think chazelle took that kind of approach, I just think he aimed really high looking at the finger but forgetting about the moon. It's a way of saying that means he just focused, imho clearly, on the wrong things, for large chunks of the movie. I feel like this movie HAD to be three hours long st least for him to make sense, but actually it's just way too long and messy this way, and the epic scope is lost. I really don't think Akerman and Cassavetes' films are at all comparable. There is no ground, no rules, no filmmaking establishment broken or put into discussion here, just a lot of muscle flexing and shock value. 

Why he chose to open the movie that way? I think he wanted to get dirty, to communicate that in this movie there will be some shit digging to do. And it was literally in your face. I really think it could have been avoided simply because it just looks distracting, but it's not what bothered me the most about it, it's the fact that it's one of the very moments where the importance of it seemed like a given to him, while it's not. It's the kind of simple thing that's very difficult to pull of: comedy. If you realize, there is almost none in his movies as of today. 

And, even if he made some very good movies as of now, and he deservedly got a good grade of praise and accolades, he's not an expert filmmaker and that is the exact reason this film got so many problems. An expert filmmaker knows when to correct stuff so the film ain't a mess, quite simply. Ego, ambition and self indulgence are what made the movie difficult for the audience and for the editor :P

Right which is why I commented that the contrast should be between the free-spirited 20s and the conservative 30s. That's a great source of conflict. The polarized reaction to this film comes from the fact that it feels like a first draft. Taking the ideas and refining them until everything connects perfectly would have made it a masterpiece.

I'd have shown the pushing out. Have Hays (or a subordinate) order Manny to replace Ruth with a male director, she's asked to train her replacement. Replacing the absurd amount of vomit with that scene would improve the movie a lot.
It didn’t

>I don't really don't think Akerman and Cassavetes' films are at all comparable. There is no ground, no rules, no filmmaking establishment broken or put into discussion here, just a lot of muscle flexing and shock value. 

I mean, of course we can't really compare Chazelle to these legendary, disruptive filmmakers. I've briefly compared how he uses exhaustion in Babylon, besides, Chazelle's influences are completely different (let's not get in that "Chazelle is a weak imitation of Demy" terrene). 

Maybe it's just me who defends the guy's work too much—it may be indulgent, it may be a fun disaster but a disaster still, and I don't want to love something blindly—but I don't feel it is much of a mess. You could say that characters aren't that profound, that it's too excessive at times, that there may be a scene you could take out from it... any kind of criticism... but the discussion all around it calling it a mess (I know you don't call it that) seems strange to me. It's not much of a lineal film for sure, feels more like anachronic, blurry memories of a time period (with its confusions and contradictions), rather than something more formal in storytelling. But the themes and subtext is there. And I feel the more I rewatch it and think about, it gets better—you get to discover the subtleties behind the distractions, as you said, an elephant shitting on a screen (maybe it's just me... I came to your same conclusions the first times I watched it, so I know where you come from).

There's this moment, for example, which seems so messy at first, so ridiculous that your first reaction is "how wasn't this cut from the movie?" I'm talking about the snake fighting scene, unnecessary and excessive on a first watch, but what you are really seeing is pure attention-seeking behaviour from Nellie, which leads to mildly serious consequences (once again, probably too stretched of an interpretation, but... isn't this film overwhelmed by manic-depression, attention-seeking too?). On the other hand, same scene, you got Brad Pitt's character who stares into the mess... lamenting a wild-west Hollywood that's fading away? Realizing his life consists of nothing more but absurd excess? The look in his eyes with Hurwitz music in the background opens a space for questions... it's a short moment of silent contemplation in a movie where our characters are being constantly stimulated, which leads to the audience being constantly stimulated too by nothing else but the film itself, which relates to an audience being stimulated by Singin' in the Rain at the film's ending, leading to an audience watching Avatar, and an audience watching Babylon... and slowly we see Hollywood holding the strings of a machinery which results we fall in a wonder to. And how long will this machine last? After the ending montage, Chazelle seems to fuck around with the film itself (in fact, in an interview or podcast he said that this wasn't even on the script, and said that it wasn't a movie wasn't trying to be normal, that it needed more (yes, he simply said that, so should we call the montage pretensious? Or was Chazelle suddenly enlightened, guided by his most primitive filmmaking-intuitions?)). I'm still trying to figure it out. I don't know if to like or dislike his abstraction. Sometimes an artist makes decisions and doesn't really know why, what was going on on Chazelle's unconscious?

About the elephant, yes, it may be a silly joke. Also Chazelle telling the audience: I don't care.

Anyways, it's just an interpretation which may change with more viewings. The reviews I've referenced in the post and it the comments say much more and with much better prose.

>And, even if he made some very good movies as of now, and he deservedly got a good grade of praise and accolades, he's not an expert filmmaker and that is the exact reason this film got so many problems. An expert filmmaker knows when to correct stuff so the film ain't a mess, quite simply. Ego, ambition and self indulgence are what made the movie difficult for the audience and for the editor :P

When I say he's an expert filmmaker, I mean it in a way that he made extremely successful films, both in critics an audience—anyone interested, not even in film but entertainment in general, recognizes Whiplash and La La Land as great works of the last decade. Maybe "expert" is not the right word... also, I don't wanna use reception as a way of measuring a work of art. But I do believe that right now he's one of the best filmmakers coming from Hollywood; not because of his single-takes and whip-pans, but because even when some film of him may be messy, the subjects it brings to the table, and the poetry he brings them with, is something to highlight.
Thanks, I'll read it later!

You mentioned above that you don’t think Chazelle could’ve crafted this any tighter.  If anything, I think your entire premise here is that the film is SUPPOSED to be a big, bloated mess.  I felt like I understood his vision but he didn’t really nail the landing.  

You acknowledge you can’t know his motivations, so you’re taking A LOT of guesses that I think are answers to criticisms of the film.  I think there’s some truth in your arguments and I wouldn’t be surprised if some of the choices Chazelle made were explained through them.

I think the whole case falls apart if you look at the movie through the lens you are using and then take a step back and think of ways that idea could’ve been executed 100x more effectively.  If Chazelle wanted to showcase how soulless the movie business is and how none of these characters really matter; then make that movie.  I think there’s a LOT of material in the film that was written in order to help fully flesh out the characters and ultimately make us feel sorry for them and hate the big Hollywood machine.  But I didn’t end up feeling anything for them.  I think when your mention the intentional “cold” nature of film…I don’t think that was intentional.  There was a genuine attempt to make us connect with the characters but there was just too many ideas and too much going on for it to work.  You could cut an hour out of the film and probably showcase the points you think Chazelle was trying to make much more effectively.  

Hollywood chews people up and spits them out and leaves everyone unhappy (or dead).  If that’s the thesis of the movie, you either need to actually make the audience care about the struggle OR you go in an even more meta direction and really hammer home the point that these characters mean nothing and then at least the audience could feel sad or feel SOMETHING by the end of the film.

It’s well shot and some of the performances were great.  I just think it was a huge swing and Chazelle is not in a league of filmmakers that could take on such a challenge successfully.  

And by the end of the film, after we’ve learned how the evil Hollywood machine works we get the dumbest montage of all-time that’s supposed to be a love letter of sorts to cinema? Like, “Yeah, the business is brutal but look at all the cool shit we get from it!”.  Movies are cool and pain is the price of admission.  But we don’t end up feeling any of the pain, so what’s the point?  You bring up the “cold” nature of the film a few times, which is a fair argument.  But at the very least you want to illicit emotion in the audience.  There are dozens and dozens of cruel/cold films that are able to leave you feeling like you just got shot in the heart.  I didn’t feel anything by the end of Babylon.  My only takeaway was that Chazelle will probably never get a budget like that again lol. 

Again, I think you want to make the movie your describing, you just have to go in a more self aware direction if you want the audience to connect.
[removed]
Didn't read your shit. La La Land was bad because the dancing was bad.

>I think there’s a LOT of material in the film that was written in order to help fully flesh out the characters and ultimately make us feel sorry for them and hate the big Hollywood machine.

Despite my exhaustive readings, what you're saying makes sense, in a way. I have this feeling that Chazelle's intention wasn't to fully flesh out MOST characters, or at least not to the extent we would expect. When I think of Sidney, for example, I think of a guy who wanted to be a successful musician, but realized that it was not worth it to break his identity trying to fit into Hollywood, and found personal success away from it, in a remote bar playing music he was fond of. Now, in my opinion, that's pretty great writing. Maybe the downside is that we don't really get to know him—we have extremely short interactions with other band members that I don't even know if they can be referred as friends, we don't know about his family, about his life outside his work/passion, etc.—, so it seems that Sidney becomes just a vehicle for Chazelle to expand on a bigger subject (well, that's in a way, essentially what a character is), but you can also blame ("blame") Chazelle of making an extreme reduction of a character who is black to drive themes about racism in Hollywood. But then again, when I think of Sidney, I'm not only thinking of racism, but I also think of someone who was strong, followed his own values, and respected/loved himself enough by not becoming something less of who he is.

Is this considered "good" character writing? Is it acceptable? Is it empty? Too basic, simplified or even ignorant? If Chazelle's intentions were to make of Sidney's character's roughly what I said, he probably achieved something. He didn't just do that with Sydney, but more or less with every character in the story.

Well, you know I've already said it. What happens is that behind all this mess Chazelle is showing us—orgy parties, film-studios, snake-fights—, real emotions seems to remain "hidden". To me, it felt like he was jumping the shark. He set out to make a Art House film and the montage was something “artsy” he decided to throw in.  In my experience, trying to be artsy/different doesn’t always translate to good material.  

I think that’s where the film school comparison comes in, it’s a bunch of kids trying weird stuff and then realizing, “Oh, the reason I’ve never seen that before is because it’s dumb.”  But Chazelle used it anyway.  

I don’t think there was much self awareness in the sense that the montage was all connected to the struggle of the characters in the movie. Seeing Avatar pop up completely took me out of the moment for sure, and it’s just weird there’s actual frames of the movie Avatar in Babylon, forever lol. 

Now, if Chazelle was intentionally making choices like that to be divisive, he succeeded.  Unfortunately, I didn’t feel like that was the case.  He nabbed an Oscar at a really young age and I think he was chasing another one by throwing some love to Hollywood.  The movie feels less like a critique of Hollywood and more of a, “Look at all the shit we’ve put up with to make it to this point.  Pat yourselves on the back Academy Members.”

I *just* don’t think it’s a very good movie overall.  Which sucks cause I think there’s an idea and a vision there that could’ve been something great.
